extracted.intended_audience: journalists and general readers interested in global press censorship
extracted.subtask_description: A country-by-country Associated Press survey describing censorship practices, restrictions, and pressures on foreign correspondents and domestic presses around the world, with examples of methods and notable incidents. Useful for understanding what topics are restricted, how censorship is enforced, and where press freedom is maintained or curtailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soviet Union censorship restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign correspondents in Moscow can't send dispatches unless they first appear in Soviet newspapers; banned topics include air disasters, specific information on Soviet prices, crowded housing conditions, details on personal lives of Soviet leaders; anything about Stalin may take 24 to 48 hours to clear censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correspondents have extremely limited freedom; many items are blocked or delayed and domestic press is totally subservient to the Communist dictatorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communist China total information control
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chinese mainland is sealed off from the West; everything sent out is censored and prepared as propaganda to hide or subvert facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only party-line or pro-Red writers admitted; material follows the party line faithfully (including Peiping radio).

rubrics_metrics.name: Satellite-nations controlled official news flow
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Cominform nations and satellites, most news comes from official radio broadcasts or copies of the rigidly-controlled press which reach the outside world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign observers must sift through propaganda; valuable facts are often hidden 'between the lines' and require careful reading of all material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda-reading technique for reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Alert newsmen must 'read everything' because propaganda often puts facts between the lines or buries them in drivel; scanning large amounts of material can reveal revealing disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey advice from AP correspondents: patient sifting of hundreds of pages can bring the truth into focus; don't ignore apparently irrelevant or propagandistic copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control ('calling on the carpet') censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice of summoning a correspondent after his stories are in print to exert control or demand explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form of post-publication pressure acts as a deterrent and a form of censorship even when outgoing copy is not formally blocked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banning and seizure of newspaper editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments may seize whole editions of newspapers (e.g., France: communist or pro-communist papers had editions seized on charges of inciting public disorder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seizure is used as a punitive and preventive tool and may not result in permanent closure but silences specific content temporarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government ownership/control of communication channels
rubrics_metrics.description: State-owned posts, telephone and telegraph systems reserve the right to monitor and censor dispatches (noted for France and other countries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where formal censorship is absent, control over transmission infrastructure allows governments to monitor and sometimes block or delay material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional guarantees vs proposed limits (Switzerland)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some countries (Switzerland) constitutionally guarantee press freedom and forbid censorship, though commissions may study proposals to spell out limits for misuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal protections exist but can be subject to political debate about boundaries; guarantees do not always prevent informal pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: No censorship but liability/responsibility rules (Portugal, Spain)
rubrics_metrics.description: No direct censorship of outgoing dispatches, but correspondents or domestic press may be held responsible for what they write; domestic press may be government-controlled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility laws chill reporting because writers or outlets can face penalties after publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening of seizure grounds (Italy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Italy permits no censorship on outgoing news, but the government has approved measures broadening the basis on which periodicals may be seized — e.g., for vilifying the head of state, the Pope, revealing state secrets, inciting soldiers to disobey laws, or praising fascism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal legal expansions create new pretexts for seizure beyond obscenity or immorality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and publication restrictions (West Germany)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign correspondents and the German press are not censored, but occupation authorities can ban publications that endanger prestige/security of military forces; allied troop strength and related defense matters are classified as secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Security classifications can functionally restrict reporting on defense and military topics even without general censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict government directives on editorial content (East Germany)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials, news stories and pictures must conform to directives issued by the government's information office; correspondents assigned to foreign posts must be Communists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized ideological control enforces uniformity and restricts independent reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: No formal censorship but reprisals for foreign criticism (Yugoslavia)
rubrics_metrics.description: No direct censorship of outgoing dispatches, but foreign newsmen who criticize government policy find themselves attacked in official press; domestic press under tight control though local editors may have some leeway on local affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reprisals and negative official campaigns act as indirect censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: No censorship of outgoing dispatches (Austria, several nordic countries, Netherlands, Luxembourg, Greece, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark)
rubrics_metrics.description: These countries report no censorship of outgoing dispatches for accredited foreign correspondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom of outgoing transmission does not preclude other pressures; this is an explicit positive indicator of press freedom in the survey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision or informal pressure on nationals' reporting (Pakistan, Ceylon, Pakistan supervision noted)
rubrics_metrics.description: No direct censorship of outgoing or incoming dispatches, but government 'supervision' or attempts to curb resident correspondents' writings occur; nationals' reporting may be supervised especially on critical subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervision can limit what national reporters write even when foreign correspondents are freer.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of emergency censorship (Malaya, Thailand)
rubrics_metrics.description: In states of emergency or during coups, censorship may be invoked temporarily; Malaya under emergency had strong censorship of local press regarding the anti-communist war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergency powers frequently expand government control over the press for security reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military/colonial censors (Indochina/French military)
rubrics_metrics.description: Military censors (e.g., the French military in Indochina) control political subjects and sometimes outgoing dispatches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military oversight of news in conflict zones constrains reporting on political and military matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: No censorship but informal monitoring of sources (Philippines, Japan)
rubrics_metrics.description: No formal censorship in some countries, but governments may tighten control over sources of information; Japan has no censorship of domestic press and a rigid press code emphasizing accuracy; Korean War copy is subject to censorship in Korea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial codes and source control can shape reporting standards and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility censorship (Iran)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign correspondents operate under 'responsibility' censorship: outgoing news is not routinely bothered but correspondents may be called to ministries and warned against repeating objectionable stories; residence permits may be refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government uses warnings and visa controls to influence reporting without formal prior censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws against harming national dignity (Turkey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Law provides punishment for anyone who harms the dignity of the nation or its leaders; government-supported news agencies exercise tight control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal sanctions for 'dignity' or 'insult' produce a chilling effect on critical reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military/security-only censorship (Israel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship imposed since 1948 refers only to matters of military security; dispatches for publication abroad must still be submitted to the censor for scrutiny on the military security angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited, subject-matter-specific censorship affects reporting on security topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visa and access as tools of censorship (Afghanistan, Saudi Arabia, Libya, Sudan, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: No official censorship in some places, but foreign correspondents who write unfavorably are denied visas or have difficulty returning; some countries give no welcome to foreign correspondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denying access functions as de facto censorship by preventing on-the-ground reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict incoming dispatch censorship and bans (Tunisia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship is imposed on all incoming dispatches and everything published locally; a staff of censors reads incoming newspapers and frequently bans particular issues; certain imported newspapers or magazines are forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control of incoming material prevents domestic exposure to outside reporting and eliminates foreign press influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and clearance via communications companies (Venezuela, Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign correspondents take copy to communications companies which must clear political items with government authorities prior to transmission; companies may censor stories in whole or part without informing the correspondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private or semi-private communications firms act as gatekeepers under government pressure, enabling unofficial censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal limits on criticizing allied/friendly countries (Peru)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 1949 decree forbids criticism of a country with which Peru has friendly relations; censorship keeps a watchful eye on outgoing copy and can bring correspondents to government offices for reprimand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diplomatic-protection laws limit international reporting and criticism to preserve state relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press closures, arrests and jail sentences for libel (Lebanon, Argentina, others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments may suspend papers, jail editors for libel (e.g., Lebanon: editor sentenced to 14 months), or close papers; these are used to punish criticism of government actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal libel and suspension are enforcement tools that severely constrain press freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of economic controls and resource rationing to suppress press (Argentina - newsprint rationing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Government control over newsprint imports/deliveries and rationing (as in Argentina) can be used to limit the opposition press and restrict freedom of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic levers like control of supplies are subtle but powerful methods to reduce independent press capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship via deportation or non-renewal of permits (Iranian/London Times example, Italy expulsion of Pravda correspondent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondents may be expelled, deported or refused residence permit renewals as punishment for unfavorable reporting (e.g., a London Times correspondent refused renewal; Italy ordered expulsion of a Soviet correspondent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative actions against journalists serve to intimidate the foreign press and deter critical coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential stop-orders and passport travel controls (U.S. State Department practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential stop-order procedures can be used to prevent departure of U.S. citizens on reports from security sources; passports can be stamped 'not valid for travel' to certain countries unless specifically authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travel restrictions and secret administrative orders can restrict journalists' and citizens' freedom to travel and report internationally; wrongful use prompts demands for safeguards and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press campaigns and legal reforms as victories against censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful press campaigns and militant editors can secure victories such as release of jailed journalists, resignation of officials, or repeal/amendment of censorious clauses (e.g., Chile campaign got four newsmen released and a cabinet minister resigned; Trinidad campaign led to an amendment protecting fair and accurate reports of legislative proceedings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organized journalistic resistance and public protest can reverse or limit censorship measures; these are cited as 'heartened victories' in the survey.
